source_text: Et post modicum addis: Quoniam natura humana, quae nascitur vel de coniugio vel de adulterio, Dei opus est. Quae, si malum esset, non esset generanda, si malum non haberet, non esset regeneranda; atque ut ad unum verbum utrumque concludam, natura humana, si malum esset, salvanda non esset; si ei mali nihil inesset, salvanda non esset. Qui ergo dicit eam bonum non esse, bonum negat conditae Creatorem; qui vero negat ei malum inesse, misericordem vitiatae invidet Salvatorem. Quapropter in hominibus nascentibus nec excusanda sunt adulteria per bonum, quod inde a Conditore bono creatum est, nec accusanda coniugia per malum, quod ibi a misericordi Salvatore sanandum est [n192] . Haec tam multa, quae de tuis scriptis posui, quoniam grandem in his aerumnam cogitationis pertuleras, ut acute aliquid dicere videreris, et ex more nostro, quo versute nihil agimus, et ex veritatis securitate, quoniam tuis sermonibus vix intellegi queunt, nostra oportet repetitione distingui. Dixisti ergo Manichaeos carnis vituperare naturam atque asserere hominem factum ex commixtione duarum naturarum, unius bonae, alterius malae, nos autem, quos haereticos vocas, dicere a bono Deo conditam humanam naturam testimonio auctoris sui bonam in infantibus ita esse sanam, ut Christi non habeant necessariam medicinam, te autem dicere bonam quidem a Deo bono conditam aliquando Adae fuisse naturam, sed tamen peccato esse vitiatam et ideo Christi indigere medicina. In primo quidem libro praesentis operis, quam nullo distaret fides vestra a Manichaeorum profanitate, quippe ex qua eam natam esse manifestum est, iunctis amborum opinionibus indicavi, ubi apparuit Ioviniano te per timorem copulari, Manichaeo autem omnino per amorem. Hoc ergo etiam in praesenti nobis genere disserendum est, sed prius nostra, post vestra distinguo. Verum ergo dixisti nos dicere a bono Deo naturam humanam bonam conditam, sed huc usque nostrum est; unam enim partem, qua suppletur nostra sententia, aut non vidisti aut suppressisti, aliam autem de tuo, cum non sit nostra, posuisti; nos enim non solum dicimus naturam hominis bonam a Deo esse conditam in Adam, sed in omnibus parvulis bonam ab eo Deo condi, qui primi illius auctor fuit, propter quod illum omnium hominum asserimus conditorem.
pass_a_gloss: And after a little you add: Since human nature, which is born either from marriage or from adultery, is the work of God. Which, if it were evil, would not be to be generated; if it did not have evil, would not be to be regenerated; and that I may conclude both to one word, human nature, if it were evil, would not be to be saved; if nothing of evil were in it, it would not be to be saved. Whoever therefore says it is not a good denies a good Creator of the founded; but whoever denies evil is in it begrudges a merciful Savior to the vitiated. For which reason in humans being born neither are adulteries to be excused through the good which from there has been created by the good Founder, nor are marriages to be accused through the evil which there is to be healed by the merciful Savior. These so many things which I have placed from your writings, since in these you had borne a great toil of thought, that you might seem to say something acute, both from our custom by which we do nothing craftily, and from the security of truth, since they can scarcely be understood by your speeches, it is fitting they be distinguished by our repetition. You have said therefore that the Manichaeans vituperate the nature of flesh and assert a human made from the mixture of two natures, of one good, of the other evil, but we, whom you call heretics, say that human nature founded by the good God is good by the testimony of its author, in infants so healthy that they do not have the necessary medicine of Christ, but you say that the nature of Adam was indeed once founded good by the good God, but nevertheless has been vitiated by sin and therefore needs the medicine of Christ. In the first book indeed of the present work, how your faith differed in nothing from the profanity of the Manichaeans, from which indeed it is manifest it was born, I indicated by joining the opinions of both, where it appeared that you are copulated to Jovinian through fear, but to the Manichaean altogether through love. This therefore must also be discoursed by us in the present kind, but first I distinguish ours, afterward yours. You have said true therefore that we say human nature was founded good by the good God, but up to here it is ours; for one part by which our sentence is supplied you either have not seen or have suppressed, but another from your own, since it is not ours, you have placed; for we not only say the nature of a human was founded good by God in Adam, but in all little ones it is founded good by that God who was the author of that first one, on account of which we assert him the founder of all humans.

pass_b_english: A little later you add: ‘Human nature, whether born from marriage or adultery, is God’s work. If it were evil, it should not be generated; if it had no evil, it should not be regenerated. To sum up both points in one word: if human nature were evil, it ought not to be saved; if no evil were within it, it would not need to be saved. Whoever says it is not good denies a good Creator to the nature that was created. Whoever denies it contains evil begrudges a merciful Savior to the nature that was corrupted. Therefore, in the birth of human beings, adultery must not be excused because of the good created from it by the good Creator; nor must marriage be condemned because of the evil that the merciful Savior must heal there’ (Augustine, Marriage and Sexual Desire 2.36).

I have quoted these many passages from your writings, in which you endured great labor of thought to seem to say something clever. In keeping with our practice of using no tricks, and in confidence in the truth, they ought to be distinguished through our restatement, because your words are scarcely intelligible. You said, then, that the Manichaeans condemn flesh’s nature and maintain that humanity was made by mixing two natures, one good and the other evil. You said that we, whom you call heretics, say human nature was made by the good God and is good on its maker’s testimony, but is so healthy in infants that they do not need Christ’s medicine. Your own claim is that Adam’s nature was once good, made by the good God, but was corrupted by sin and therefore needs Christ’s medicine.

In the first book of this work I set your opinions beside the Manichaeans’ and showed that your faith differed in no way from their irreverence, from which it clearly sprang. There it appeared that fear unites you with Jovinian, but love wholly unites you with Mani. We must discuss this in the present context too, but first I distinguish our views, then yours. You correctly said we maintain that the good God made human nature good. But only this much is ours. You either failed to notice or suppressed one part needed to complete our position and inserted another of your own that is not ours. For we do not merely say God made human nature good in Adam. We say that in all infants it is created good by the same God who made that first human being. That is why we affirm that he creates all people.

choices.why: Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
Julian defends marriage as God's work against the charge that generation transmits sin.
